contributions.headingText: Composite phaeochromocytoma/paraganglioma is a tumour composed of a phaeochromocytoma/paraganglioma and one or more developmentally related tumour(s) such as ganglioneuroma, ganglioneuroblastoma, neuroblastoma, or peripheral nerve sheath tumour.

Adrenal

Composite phaeochromocytoma-ganglioneuroma; composite phaeochromocytoma-ganglioneuroblastoma; composite phaeochromocytoma-neuroblastoma; composite phaeochromocytoma–peripheral nerve sheath tumour

Extra-adrenal

Composite paraganglioma-neuroblastoma; composite paraganglioma-ganglioneuroblastoma

Paediatric composite tumours occur slightly more commonly on the right side, with multiple tumours possible {32508744}. The majority of composite tumours in paediatric populations are composite phaeochromocytomas, with only three composite paragangliomas reported {19251979; 32508744}. Composite paragangliomas develop in the retroperitoneum and mediastinum in children {19251979; 32508744}, different from the retroperitoneal and urinary bladder localization in adults {12114785; 24144290}.

Most composite tumours are functional, although levels of catecholamines vary. Patients may present with WDHA syndrome (watery diarrhoea, hypokalaemia, and achlorhydria) caused by the production of serum-detected VIP. Paroxysmal high blood pressure may manifest as headache and sweating. An abdominal mass may also be detected {20162688}. Diagnosis can be confirmed by endocrinological investigations (increased blood and urine catecholamines) and radiological investigations (CT, MRI, and MIBG), with PET-CT aiding in the detection of metastatic lesions.

Composite phaeochromocytoma/paraganglioma is extremely rare {12114771; 24144290; 28752484; 31966391}, with about 7% of cases identified in paediatric patients {32508744; 28864906; 22440998; 20162688; 19864235; 19251979; 17727489; 16481267; 3667875}. Paediatric composite tumours are slightly more common in girls {24144290}.

Both the neuroendocrine and neural elements have a common embryogenic origin in the neural crest. Tumours that have one component initially and later develop another component during the clinical course have been reported {22440998; 32508744; 17727489}. Any tumour with a component of phaeochromocytoma/paraganglioma is considered an indication for genetic testing {29239044}. With > 25 different genes implicated in the pathogenesis of phaeochromocytoma/paraganglioma, the degree of testing should be determined by local resources and pretest probabilities {26839173; 29239044}. Germline mutations appear to be less common in composite tumours than in pure phaeochromocytoma/paraganglioma. However, NF1 and MAX mutations have been reported {32508744; 19251979; 3667875; 19864235}, along with SDHB deletion {19251979; 29239034}. Rare composite phaeochromocytoma may be seen in neurofibromatosis type 1 {19864235}. MYCN amplification is a poor prognostic factor in neuroblastoma {16941154} and has been reported in composite phaeochromocytoma-neuroblastoma {28864906}.

The cut surface is heterogeneous, with distinct components visible that match the different components: brown areas with haemorrhage (chromaffin tumour) mixed with tan areas (neural tumour) {22440998}. Cystic change may be seen {20162688}. The median tumour diameter is 60 mm (range: 35–150 mm).

A composite tumour requires the presence of well-developed cytological and architectural features of both a phaeochromocytoma/paraganglioma component and another embryologically related (i.e. not cortical) tumour type. The presence of a few isolated ganglion cells or a small amount of Schwannian stroma in an otherwise typical phaeochromocytoma/paraganglioma does not warrant classification as a composite tumour. A useful rule of thumb is that ≥ 5% of the tumour should be composed of each tumour type. In paediatric populations, the neural component is most often neuroblastoma and less frequently ganglioneuroblastoma or ganglioneuroma. Neuroblastoma is identified by the immature neuroblastic cells with focal rosette-like arrangement and background neuropil. Schwannian stroma and ganglion cells are noted in ganglioneuroblastoma or ganglioneuroma, whereas streaming fascicles of elongated tumour cells with myxoid stroma are noted when the second tumour is malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour {17727489}. Paediatric composite tumours may spread to lymph nodes {3667875}, liver, lung, and bones {3667875; 22440998}. Metastatic foci may contain one or both components {3667875; 28864906; 32508744; 22440998}, although in composite phaeochromocytoma–malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour, metastatic foci consisted exclusively of one component or the other, with metastatic phaeochromocytoma in the bones and malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour in the liver, lungs, and lymph nodes {17727489}.

Immunohistochemistry

Phaeochromocytoma/paraganglioma shows vimentin reactivity, with sustentacular cells positive for GFAP and S100, whereas neuroblastoma is negative or only focally positive for these markers {16481267}. VIP protein may be identified in patients with WDHA syndrome.
Essential: presence of cytologically and architecturally recognizable phaeochromocytoma/paraganglioma differentiation and a neural component; minor component constituting ≥ 5% of tumour volume.

In contrast to composite tumours in adults, in which metastases are uncommon {31966391; 19829717; 28752484; 11376017}, > 55% of paediatric composite tumours have metastases {28864906; 22440998; 17727489; 3667875; 32508744}.
